clue.text: What's confused by me — bleach and milky sauce!

indicators.note: confused letters are jumbled up, so the words me and bleach are to be rearranged together

explanation.surface: Someone baffled that bleach and a creamy sauce look so alike, exclaiming in mock dismay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' tells you to rearrange ME and BLEACH as one pool of letters; 'What's ... by' and 'and' are just joining words.
explanation.definitionFit: Béchamel is the classic French white sauce made from a roux and milk.

clue.text: Tempted more than once, dumping wife in the end

indicators.note: in places the trimmed word inside the word for the end

parts.note: the end is simply END

indicators.note: dumping the wife means the letter standing for wife is dropped from the word for more than once

parts.note: twice is more than once

explanation.surface: Someone lured into temptation repeatedly, finally abandoning his wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'more than once' is TWICE; 'dumping wife' drops its W, and 'in' sets the remainder inside 'the end' taken literally.
explanation.definitionFit: To entice is to lure or tempt someone with something attractive.

clue.text: Meat was preserved from a flood

definitions.meaning: cured pork from a pig's leg
in Genesis, Noah's son of this name was saved from the Flood in the ark

explanation.walkthrough: 'preserved' suggests curing meat, which fits the first sense, but the second definition is biblical: Noah's sons Shem, Ham and Japheth survived the Flood.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both cured pork meat and the name of one of Noah's three sons, saved in the ark.

clue.text: Insincere man had strange sort of language

indicators.note: strange implies something odd and altered, so the letters of insincere man had are rearranged

explanation.surface: A two-faced fellow who spoke in an odd kind of tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges the fifteen letters of INSINCERE MAN HAD.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the most widely spoken variety of Chinese, the official standard tongue of China.

clue.text: Print seen in literary house

parts.note: LIT is the common abbreviation for literary

explanation.surface: A print spotted hanging in a bookish household.
explanation.definitionFit: A litho is a lithograph, a picture printed from a flat stone or metal plate.

clue.text: It's astoundin' when duck displaces one in river

indicators.note: displaces means the duck's letter pushes out and takes the place of the letter for one

parts.note: amazin' is a dropped-g way of saying astounding
I is the Roman numeral for one
a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, so O

explanation.surface: A folksy exclamation of wonder at a duck turning up on a river.
explanation.walkthrough: In AMAZIN', 'displaces' swaps the I for O, a cricket duck being a zero score. The apostrophe in 'astoundin'' hints that the synonym also drops its final G.
explanation.definitionFit: The Amazon is the great South American river.

clue.text: What spokesperson of large organisation may have — the burden of many bad actions?

definitions.text: What spokesperson of large organisation may have
definitions.meaning: read literally: a great many queries to reply to on the firm's behalf

definitions.text: the burden of many bad actions?
definitions.meaning: the idiom for being responsible for much wrongdoing

explanation.definitionFit: Literally, a heap of queries needing replies; idiomatically, being to blame for many misdeeds.

clue.text: A day given to work — after that, there's a party drink

parts.note: MON is short for Monday, a day
to till is to work the soil
a do is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: Someone spends a day at work, then heads off to a party for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The day is Monday, shortened, and 'work' is the farming sense, to work the land; 'after that, there's' only carries the charade on in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Amontillado is a medium-dry Spanish sherry, a fortified wine.

clue.text: Set of principles — what the church musician must have if he's to play?

definitions.meaning: a body of logical rules or method, as in Aristotle's logical works

definitions.text: what the church musician must have if he's to play?
definitions.meaning: a church keyboard player needs his instrument switched on, read as two words

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the answer into two words: the instrument plus 'on', as it must be before anyone can play it.
explanation.definitionFit: An organon is a system of rules for reasoning; split, the letters say the church instrument is switched on.

clue.text: A contributor to stamina!

parts.note: in Latin the word for vigour is a plural, so each singular thread contributes to it; botanically, a pollen-bearing flower part

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark flags the trick: the English word stamina began as the Latin plural, so one of these is a single contributor to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Stamina is the Latin plural of this word, originally meaning a thread or warp; it is also the male part of a flower.

clue.text: Finished, with nothing skipped over?

indicators.note: with here means the letter for nothing is set within the word for finished

parts.note: through means done or finished, as in 'I'm through'
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Asking whether a task is done completely, with no step left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer, and it also builds it: O (nothing) goes inside THROUGH (finished).
explanation.definitionFit: A thorough job is complete in every detail, leaving no part neglected.

clue.text: Perhaps cats make a search

parts.note: the word cats is what you get from the letters of cast moved about, so the clue word is wordplay for the phrase

explanation.surface: A suggestion that cats might be the ones doing the hunting.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read 'CAST ABOUT' as an instruction, rearranging CAST, and the result is CATS. 'Perhaps' signals that cats is just one possible result.
explanation.definitionFit: To cast about is to look around in all directions for something.

clue.text: Old monument simulated by electronics

indicators.note: something simulated is a made-up version, so the letters of electronics are reworked into a new shape

explanation.surface: An ancient site recreated as a computer model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'simulated' rearranges the eleven letters of ELECTRONICS.
explanation.definitionFit: A stone circle is a prehistoric ring of standing stones, such as Stonehenge.

clue.text: French fashion with English feel

parts.note: ton is the French word for style or fashion, as in bon ton

explanation.surface: French chic given an English character.
explanation.definitionFit: The tone of a place or event is its general feel or atmosphere.

clue.text: Not all fodder is sent back — this is edible

indicators.note: sent back means the run taken from fodder is read in reverse
not all of the word fodder is used, only a run of letters inside it

explanation.surface: Not every bit of animal feed is returned, since some is fit to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not all' takes ODDE from inside fODDEr and 'sent back' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: An eddo is the starchy tuber of the taro plant, eaten as a vegetable.

clue.text: Establishing home that's big, with grass around

parts.note: in means at home

indicators.note: around means the word for grass wraps round the word for big

parts.note: to grass, or sing, is to inform on someone to the police
tall means big in height

explanation.surface: Setting up in a large house surrounded by lawns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grass' is the British slang verb for informing on someone to the police, the same as singing; 'around' wraps it round the word for big.
explanation.definitionFit: Installing someone or something means putting it in place, setting it up.

clue.text: Girl is fat — tons to be shed!

indicators.note: to be shed means the letter for tons is lost from the word for fat

parts.note: suet is hard animal fat used in cooking

explanation.surface: A remark that a young woman is overweight and needs to lose a great deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be shed' drops T from SUET.
explanation.definitionFit: Sue is a girl's name, short for Susan.

clue.text: Welsh caterers supply Swansea's foremost low-calorie food

indicators.note: read as the adverb of supple, flexibly, so the letters of caterers bend into a new order
foremost means the opening letter of Swansea is taken

explanation.surface: Caterers in Wales provide a Swansea favourite that is light on calories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supply' looks like the verb, but here it is the adverb from supple, meaning flexibly, and it shows CATERERS being rearranged. S, the first letter of Swansea, ends the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Watercress is a peppery salad leaf with almost no calories.

clue.text: A north American rejecting an early settler in his country

indicators.note: rejecting means the word an is thrown out of the nationality

parts.note: a Canadian is a North American

explanation.surface: A Canadian disowning someone who settled his land long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejecting an' removes the word 'an' from the nationality, not a single letter. 'his' in the definition refers back to the Canadian, since Acadia lay in what is now Canada.
explanation.definitionFit: Acadians were the French colonists of Acadia, in what is now eastern Canada.

clue.text: A wife always off somewhere

parts.note: ay, or aye, is an old word for always or ever

explanation.surface: A wife who is always out somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: AY (or aye) meaning 'ever, always' is old-fashioned, but a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: To be away is to be absent, gone off to some other place.

clue.text: Herb, a citizen nabbed by officer

indicators.note: nabbed by means the citizen is seized and held inside the officer

parts.note: Lt is the abbreviation for lieutenant, an officer
Citizen Kane is the Orson Welles film, so Kane is the citizen

explanation.surface: A plant, or a member of the public arrested by a policeman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'citizen' points to the Orson Welles film Citizen Kane; 'nabbed by' puts that name inside the abbreviation for lieutenant.
explanation.definitionFit: Alkanet is a plant of the borage family whose root yields a red dye.

clue.text: Queen fled to island

parts.note: ran means fled

explanation.surface: A queen escaping to an island.
explanation.definitionFit: A rani is an Indian queen or a rajah's wife.

clue.text: Like prisoner stuck on ship in port?

definitions.text: Like prisoner stuck on ship in port?

parts.words: Like prisoner stuck on ship in port
parts.note: seems to describe a captive aboard a moored vessel, but combines the place an accused stands in court with where a ship berths

explanation.walkthrough: In a British court the dock is the enclosure where the accused stands, while a ship in port is moored in a dock.
explanation.definitionFit: A defendant stands in the enclosure of a courtroom; a ship in harbour sits in its berth.

clue.text: Connection brought by indication of public-school background at Oxford, say

parts.note: the old school tie is the emblem of having attended a public (private, fee-paying) school
up means in residence at a university, Oxford being one example

explanation.surface: A link forged by flaunting a privileged education at Oxford.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a 'public school' is a fee-paying private school, its old school tie a badge of privilege; being 'up' means being at university.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie-up is a link or business association between two parties.

clue.text: Unattached woman's going to Mediterranean island

parts.note: Di is a woman's name, so woman's gives DI'S
Crete is a Greek island in the Mediterranean

explanation.surface: A single woman off on holiday to a Greek island.
explanation.definitionFit: Discrete means separate and distinct, not joined to anything else.

clue.text: Last insignificant bit of agenda not covered

indicators.note: not covered means the outer letters of the words of agenda are stripped off, exposing the run within

explanation.surface: The final trivial item on a meeting's agenda, never reached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not covered' strips the outer letters from 'of agenda', leaving the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A fag end is the final, worthless remnant of something, like a cigarette stub.

clue.text: My horse only gets half way!

indicators.note: only half of the word for horse is kept, the opening half

parts.note: a childish word for a horse

explanation.surface: A rider's lament that their horse stops halfway round the course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is not a possessive here but an exclamation of surprise. 'only gets half way' keeps half of GEE-GEE, the nursery word for a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of surprise, as in 'My, that's big!'

clue.text: Old lover embraced by girl — a bit on the side?

indicators.note: embraced by means the old lover is held inside the girl's name

parts.note: Anne is a girl's name
an ex is a former partner

explanation.surface: A former boyfriend in a girl's arms, suggesting an affair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a bit on the side' looks like a lover, which suits the surface, but it means an extension built onto the side of a building.
explanation.definitionFit: An annexe is an extra building or extension attached to the side of a main one.

clue.text: Signs of returning bad temper outside part of the hospital

indicators.note: outside means the reversed word goes round the hospital department
returning means the word for a fit of bad temper is read backwards

parts.note: a strop is a fit of bad temper
ENT is the ear, nose and throat department of a hospital

explanation.surface: Omens of a bad mood coming back around a hospital ward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns STROP into PORTS, which goes 'outside' ENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Portents are omens, signs warning of something to come.
